questions.stem: In a two-level cache system, the access times of $L_1$ and $L_2$ caches are 1 and 8 clock cycles, respectively. The miss penalty from the $L_2$ cache to main memory is 18 clock cycles. The miss rate of $L_1$ cache is twice that of $L_2$. The average memory access time (AMAT) of this cache system is 2 cycles. The miss rates of $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively are:

solutionDiagram.alt: A chain CPU, L1 at 1 cycle with miss rate 2x, L2 at 8 cycles with miss rate x, memory at 18 cycles; solving the AMAT equation gives x = 1/18.

steps.title: Miss rate, miss penalty and AMAT for two levels
steps.body: The miss rate of a cache is the fraction of the accesses that reach that cache which miss it. The miss penalty of a level is the extra time its misses cost. The average memory access time (AMAT) is the expected time of one CPU access. Every access pays the L1 time. Only L1 misses go on to L2 and pay its time, and only L2 misses pay the main-memory penalty. Each level's miss rate is measured on the accesses that reach it, so the terms nest.

steps.title: Solve
steps.body: Subtract 1: $1=16x+36x^{2}$, so $36x^{2}+16x-1=0$. The discriminant is $16^2+4\cdot36=256+144=400$, with square root 20. The positive root is $x=(-16+20)/72=1/18\approx0.0556$. The negative root is not a rate.

steps.title: Read off the answer
steps.body: $m_2=1/18\approx0.056$ and $m_1=2/18=1/9\approx0.111$. Check: $1+\tfrac19\bigl(8+18\cdot\tfrac1{18}\bigr)=1+\tfrac19\cdot9=2$. That is option A, L1 first.

shortcut.body: Use the options. The AMAT equation says $m_1(8+18m_2)=1$. Option A: $0.111\times(8+1.0)=1.0$, which works at once. Keep in mind that L1 must be the larger rate, so B and C are out before any arithmetic; D has the right ratio but gives AMAT $=1+0.1784\times(8+1.61)=2.71$. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Reading "the miss rate of $L_1$ is twice that of $L_2$" backwards. Here L1 gets 0.056 and L2 0.111, so the rates are in the wrong order, and the AMAT comes to 1.56.

The pair puts the larger rate on L2 (0.1784) and the smaller on L1 (0.0892), breaking the stated 2:1 ratio. It is the exact solution of the equation for the swapped ratio, $1+x(8+36x)=2$ with $x=m_1$, so the AMAT checks out to 2 and it looks right if you read the ratio backwards.
The ratio of two to one is right, but the values do not satisfy the AMAT equation: $1+0.1784\,(8+18\times0.0892)=2.71$, not 2. Matching the ratio alone is not enough.

recognize.clues: Two cache levels with their own access times, a memory penalty, a given average access time and a ratio between the two miss rates. The unknowns are the rates, so the nested time formula is solved backwards.
recognize.contrast: A forward AMAT question gives both rates and asks for the time. Here the time is given and the rates are unknown, so you must form and solve an equation, and the order of the 2:1 ratio matters.

check.body: Test the swapped pair, $m_1=1/18$ and $m_2=1/9$: $1+\tfrac1{18}(8+18\cdot\tfrac19)=1+\tfrac{10}{18}\approx1.56$, not 2. So the equation, and not only the 2:1 ratio, fixes which rate is larger.

questions.stem:
The read access times and the hit ratios for different caches in a memory hierarchy are as given below.

The read access time of main memory is 90 nanoseconds. Assume that the caches use the referred-word-first read policy and the write back policy. Assume that all the caches are direct mapped caches. Assume that the dirty bit is always 0 for all the blocks in the caches. In execution of a program, 60% of memory reads are for instruction fetch and 40% are for memory operand fetch. The average read access time in nanoseconds (up to 2 decimal places) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Instruction fetches go to the I-cache and operand fetches to the D-cache; both L1 caches miss into one shared L2 and then memory. Path costs 5.4 ns and 3.7 ns give 4.72 ns.

steps.title: Terms in the question and the one rule
steps.body: The hit ratio of a cache is the fraction of reads it satisfies; the others miss and go to the next level. The read access time is the time to read when the level hits. Referred-word-first means the requested word is passed to the processor as soon as it arrives, without waiting for the rest of the block, so no extra block-fill time is added. Write back with the dirty bit always 0 means no victim ever has to be written out on a miss, so there is no write-back cost. What remains is the nesting rule: the average read time of a level is its own access time plus its miss ratio times the average read time of the level below.

steps.title: Cost of an L1 miss
steps.body: The I-cache and the D-cache both miss into the same L2, which has access time 8 ns and hit ratio 0.9; its own misses go to memory at 90 ns. So the cost seen by any L1 miss is $T_{L2}=8+0.1\times90=17$ ns.

steps.title: Instruction path and data path
steps.body: Instruction fetch: $2+(1-0.8)\times17=2+3.4=5.4$ ns. Operand fetch: $2+(1-0.9)\times17=2+1.7=3.7$ ns.

steps.title: Mix the two paths
steps.body: $60\%$ of reads are instructions and $40\%$ are operands: $0.6\times5.4+0.4\times3.7=3.24+1.48=4.72$ ns.

shortcut.body: Mix the L1 miss ratios first: $0.6\times0.2+0.4\times0.1=0.16$ of all reads miss L1. Each miss costs 17 ns more than the 2 ns L1 time, so $2+0.16\times17=2+2.72=4.72$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Using 8 ns alone for L2 and leaving out its own misses to memory ($0.1\times90$) gives $0.6(2+0.2\times8)+0.4(2+0.1\times8)=3.28$. L2 misses must be charged the 90 ns.
Swapping the weights, 40% instructions and 60% operands, gives 4.38. The 60% belongs to instruction fetch.
Leaving L2 out and sending L1 misses straight to memory: $0.6(2+0.2\times90)+0.4(2+0.1\times90)=16.4$.

recognize.clues: Separate instruction and data caches with their own hit ratios, a shared second-level cache, memory below, and a 60/40 split of the reads. The words average read access time ask for the nested expected time.
recognize.contrast: A single-level EMAT question has one hit ratio. Here the miss branch of each first-level cache leads into another cache, so the second level must be resolved first and the 60/40 weights applied last.

check.body: Count per 1000 reads. 600 are instruction fetches and 400 are operand fetches, so $0.2\times600+0.1\times400=160$ miss the first level. Of those, $0.9\times160=144$ hit the second level and 16 go to memory. Total time: $1000\times2+160\times8+16\times90=2000+1280+1440=4720$ ns, and $4720/1000=4.72$ ns.

questions.stem: Consider a machine with a byte addressable main memory of $2^{32}$ bytes divided into blocks of size 32 bytes. Assume that a direct mapped cache having 512 cache lines is used with this machine. The size of the tag field in bits is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The 32-bit address of a direct-mapped cache with 512 lines of 32 bytes: an 18-bit tag, a 9-bit index and a 5-bit offset.

steps.title: Tag, index and offset
steps.body: A direct-mapped cache puts each memory block in exactly one line. The address is cut from the right into the offset (the byte within a block), the index (which line) and the tag (the remaining high bits, stored with each line to say which block is there). The rule: tag $=$ address bits $-$ index bits $-$ offset bits.

steps.title: Sizes
steps.body: The memory has $2^{32}$ bytes, so addresses are 32 bits. A block of $32=2^5$ bytes gives 5 offset bits. $512=2^9$ lines give 9 index bits.

steps.title: Tag
steps.body: The tag is the 18 bits that remain: $32-9-5=18$.

shortcut.body: Index plus offset address $512\times32=2^{14}$ bytes, so they use 14 bits and the tag is $32-14=18$. Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: Answering 23: subtracting only the 9 index bits and forgetting the 5 offset bits.
Answering 27: subtracting only the offset and forgetting the index.
Answering 14, the number of index and offset bits together, instead of what is left over for the tag.

recognize.clues: Memory size, block size and line count are given and the question asks for the tag width. That is a pure field-width calculation with no access sequence.
recognize.contrast: A miss-counting question uses the same split but then tracks what each line holds. Here you stop after the widths.

check.body: Add the fields back: $18+9+5=32$ bits, the whole address. Another view: there are $2^{32}/2^{5}=2^{27}$ memory blocks sharing $2^{9}$ lines, so $2^{18}$ blocks compete for each line, and telling $2^{18}$ blocks apart takes 18 bits. A 17-bit or 19-bit tag would leave the three fields summing to 31 or 33 bits, which is not the address length.

The offset picks a byte inside a block, the index picks the cache line, and the tag is stored with the line to tell which block currently sits there.
The three field widths add up to the address length, so the tag is whatever the address leaves after the index and offset bits are taken.
Get the address length from the memory size, the offset bits from the block size and the index bits from the number of lines. All three sizes are powers of two, so each width is a logarithm base 2.
The block size is $2^5$ bytes and the line count is $2^9$. Those two widths together tell you how many low bits are not part of the tag.

questions.stem: Consider a two-level cache hierarchy with L1 and L2 caches. An application incurs 1.4 memory accesses per instruction on average. For this application, the miss rate of L1 cache is 0.1; the L2 cache experiences, on average, 7 misses per 1000 instructions. The miss rate of L2 expressed correct to two decimal places is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Per 1000 instructions: 1400 memory accesses, 140 L1 misses that reach L2, and 7 L2 misses, giving a local L2 miss rate of 0.05.

steps.title: Miss rate of a cache that sits behind another
steps.body: The miss rate of a cache is the number of its misses divided by the number of accesses that reach it. L2 is looked at only when L1 misses, so the accesses that reach L2 are exactly the L1 misses. This local rate is what "the miss rate of L2" means. The global rate, L2 misses per CPU access, is a different and smaller number.

steps.title: Count per 1000 instructions
steps.body: With 1.4 accesses per instruction, 1000 instructions make $1400$ accesses. L1 misses 10% of them: $1400\times0.1=140$ misses, and these 140 are the accesses that reach L2.

steps.title: L2 miss rate
steps.body: L2 misses 7 of those 140: $7/140=0.05$.

shortcut.body: $7\div(1000\times1.4\times0.1)=7\div140=0.05$. Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: Dividing by all 1400 accesses, $7/1400=0.005$. That is the global miss rate; the question asks for the rate of L2 on the accesses it receives.
Dividing by $1000\times0.1$ and forgetting the 1.4 accesses per instruction, which gives $7/100=0.07$.
Answering 0.007, the L2 misses per instruction. A rate is per access, not per instruction.

recognize.clues: The L2 behaviour is given as misses per 1000 instructions, while the L1 miss rate and the accesses per instruction are given separately. This mix of units asks for a conversion to a per-access rate.
recognize.contrast: The global L2 miss rate divides by all CPU accesses and the local rate divides by the L1 misses. The wording the miss rate of L2 points to the local rate.

check.body: Use the global rate as a consistency test. L2 misses are 7 per 1000 instructions, which is 1400 accesses, so the global L2 rate is $7/1400=0.005$. It must equal the L1 miss rate times the local L2 rate: $0.1\times0.05=0.005$.

variation.stem: A two-level cache hierarchy has L1 and L2 caches. An application makes 1.5 memory accesses per instruction on average. The miss rate of L1 is 0.08, and L2 experiences 9 misses per 1000 instructions. The miss rate of L2, expressed correct to three decimal places, is ____________.

questions.stem:
Consider a 2-way set associative cache with 256 blocks and uses LRU replacement. Initially the cache is empty. Conflict misses are those misses which occur due to contention of multiple blocks for the same cache set. Compulsory misses occur due to first time access to the block. The following sequence of accesses to memory blocks

(0, 128, 256, 128, 0, 128, 256, 128, 1, 129, 257, 129, 1, 129, 257, 129)

is repeated 10 times. The number of conflict misses experienced by the cache is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The two ways of set 0 after each access of two rounds: round 1 has 3 compulsory and 2 conflict misses, round 2 has 4 conflict misses; with the second set the conflict misses total 76.

steps.title: Sets, LRU and the two kinds of miss
steps.body: A cache with $S$ sets puts memory block $b$ in set $b\bmod S$, and the lines of a set hold any of the blocks that map to it. 2-way means 2 lines per set. LRU (least recently used) means that when a set is full, the line unused for the longest time is evicted. A compulsory miss is the first ever access to a block: it must miss. In this question every other miss is a conflict miss, because the block was cached before and was pushed out by other blocks of the same set. Different sets never affect each other, so each set can be simulated alone.

steps.title: Which blocks share a set
steps.body: $256$ blocks in 2-way sets make $256/2=128$ sets. Blocks 0, 128 and 256 all have remainder 0 mod 128, so they compete for set 0. Blocks 1, 129 and 257 have remainder 1 and compete for set 1. The 16 accesses are 8 for set 0 followed by the same pattern for set 1, so the two sets behave identically.

steps.title: Round 1 in set 0
steps.body: Show the set as [older, newer]. 0: miss, [0]. 128: miss, [0,128]. 256: miss, evicts 0, [128,256]. 128: hit, [256,128]. 0: miss, evicts 256, [128,0]. 128: hit, [0,128]. 256: miss, evicts 0, [128,256]. 128: hit, [256,128]. Round 1 has 5 misses: the first three (0, 128, 256) are compulsory and the 2 later ones (0, 256) are conflict misses.

steps.title: Rounds 2 to 10 in set 0
steps.body: Each round starts with the set [256,128]. 0 misses and evicts 256; 128 hits; 256 misses and evicts 0; 128 hits; 0 misses; 128 hits; 256 misses; 128 hits. That is 4 misses, all conflict, and the set ends again as [256,128], so every later round repeats it. Block 128 is touched between every two misses, so it is never the oldest line and never evicted; blocks 0 and 256 evict each other.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Conflict misses in set 0: $2+9\times4=38$. Set 1 is identical, so $2\times38=76$. Check: all misses are $2\times(5+9\times4)=82$, of which 6 are compulsory (one per distinct block), leaving $82-6=76$.

shortcut.body: In each set block 128 stays in the cache, so only references to the other two blocks can miss: they miss every time, 4 per round, 40 in 10 rounds, plus the first access to 128. That is 41 misses per set, of which 3 are compulsory: $41-3=38$ conflict misses, and $2\times38=76$. About 2 minutes. It relies on recognising that 128 is always the most recently used of the old pair, so redo the simulation if the pattern changes.

traps.text: Answering 82, the total number of misses. The 6 compulsory misses (the first access to each of 0, 128, 256, 1, 129, 257) must be subtracted.
Answering 80, which counts every access to 0, 256, 1 and 257 as a conflict miss. The first access to each of those four blocks is a compulsory miss, so it is not a conflict.

Answering 6 or 0 by thinking the 256-block cache is big enough for 6 distinct blocks. A fully associative cache of that size would only have the 6 compulsory misses, but the set mapping forces three blocks into a 2-way set.

recognize.clues: The question defines conflict and compulsory misses and gives a repeating block sequence for an LRU cache. That means separating first-time misses from avoidable ones by simulation.
recognize.contrast: A plain hit-count question only needs the total misses. Here you must also subtract the first-time misses, and the set mapping decides which blocks interfere.

check.body: Use reuse distance in set 0. Between two uses of block 0 (or of 256) the sequence touches two other distinct blocks, for example 128 and 256 between consecutive 0s. Two other blocks fill both lines of a 2-way LRU set, so every reuse of 0 or 256 misses. Between two uses of 128 only one other block appears, so 128 stays and hits. That gives 4 misses per round on 0 and 256, matching the simulation.

A set associative cache maps a block to a set by its block number modulo the number of sets, and the blocks of one set share only that set's lines.
A first-ever access to a block is a compulsory miss. Any later miss on a block that was already loaded once is, by the definition in the question, a conflict miss.
Find the number of sets and group the blocks by set. Simulate one set with LRU order written oldest to newest through the first round, then see what state the set is in when the next round begins.
The cache has $256/2=128$ sets. Take the block numbers modulo 128 to see which blocks meet in one set.

variation.stem: A 2-way set associative cache has 128 blocks and uses LRU replacement. Initially the cache is empty. Conflict misses are misses caused by contention of several blocks for the same set, and compulsory misses are first-time accesses to a block. The sequence of block accesses (0, 64, 128, 0, 64, 128, 1, 65, 129, 1, 65, 129) is repeated 6 times. The number of conflict misses is ____________.
variation.explanation: There are 64 sets, so 0, 64, 128 share set 0 and 1, 65, 129 share set 1. Cycling three blocks through a 2-way LRU set misses on every access, so each set has $6\times6=36$ misses, 3 of them compulsory. Conflict misses are $2\times(36-3)=66$.

questions.stem: A cache memory unit with capacity of $N$ words and block size of $B$ words is to be designed. If it is designed as a direct mapped cache, the length of the TAG field is 10 bits. If the cache unit is now designed as a 16-way set-associative cache, the length of the TAG field is ____________ bits.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two address bars: the direct-mapped split with a 10-bit tag, and the 16-way split in which 4 index bits have moved into the tag, making it 14 bits.

steps.title: What the tag, index and offset are
steps.body: The address is cut into the offset (the word inside the block), the index (the set) and the tag (the rest). Direct mapped means 1 line per set, so the sets number $N/B$ (the lines). In a $k$-way cache the same $N/B$ lines are grouped in sets of $k$, so the sets number $N/(kB)$. The address length and the block size, and so the offset, do not change between designs.

steps.title: Direct-mapped split
steps.body: With $N/B$ sets the index has $\log_2(N/B)$ bits and the tag is $A-\log_2(N/B)-\log_2B=A-\log_2N=10$ bits.

steps.title: 16-way split
steps.body: Now there are $N/(16B)$ sets, so the index has $\log_2(N/B)-4$ bits: four bits fewer. The offset is unchanged, so the freed 4 bits join the tag: $10+4=14$.

shortcut.body: Going from 1-way to $k$-way adds $\log_2k$ to the tag: $10+\log_216=14$. Fifteen seconds, and the values of $N$, $B$ and the address length never matter.

traps.text: Answering 6 by subtracting 4. Grouping lines into sets removes index bits, and the tag takes them over, so the tag grows.
Answering 10, thinking the cache capacity fixed means the tag is fixed. The capacity is fixed, but the tag and index trade bits.
Answering 26 by adding 16 rather than $\log_216=4$.

recognize.clues: The same cache capacity and block size are built two ways, direct mapped and k-way, and the tag width of one is given to find the other. Only the change in associativity matters.
recognize.contrast: A direct mapped split has one line per set, so index bits equal line-number bits. In the k-way design the index counts sets, which is why it shrinks.

check.body: Try concrete sizes with a 10-bit direct mapped tag: a 22-bit address, $N=2^{12}$ words and $B=2^4$ words. Direct mapped has 256 lines, an 8-bit index and a 4-bit offset, so the tag is $22-8-4=10$. In 16-way sets there are 16 sets, a 4-bit index, and the tag is $22-4-4=14$, which matches the shortcut.
